title: Letters make the absent present
hookLine: a friend's letter brings their real traces (Letters 40)

cards: A card at the back of a drawer, in the handwriting of someone who's gone, or far away. A grandmother's loopy capitals. A friend's note on a napkin.
A photo of it would hold the words. But the paper holds something else. Lucilius writes to Seneca often, and in the fortieth letter Seneca thanks him, and tries to say what a letter actually does.

teach.b: Writing often, Seneca says, is the one way Lucilius can show himself, and every time a letter comes, the two of them are together at once. Then a comparison.
If we're glad to have pictures of absent friends, which refresh the memory and ease the longing with a comfort that is empty and false, how much gladder are we of a letter?

teach.h: A PORTRAIT IS PAINT; A LETTER IS TRACES.
teach.b: A portrait is paint. A letter carries real traces, real marks, of the friend who isn't there.
Sweetest of all, he says, it brings the friend's own handwriting: in a sense, their hand itself, pressed onto the page. Typed words can't do that.
The rest of the letter turns to how a philosopher should speak: not in a torrent, like a man he heard rushing his words, but slowly, so the listener can take it in. A letter allows exactly that.
You think before you say, and your friend reads at their own pace.
Both men are long gone, and their words still arrive, which is its own small proof that writing can make the absent present.

how: Some readers of Seneca keep up a handwritten correspondence with one friend, writing slowly and often, as he and Lucilius did.

o: the marks of a friend a letter brings, even their own hand
clues a detective finds that prove someone was there
a portrait that keeps a friend's face fresh in memory

games.q: the friend's letter — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca says a portrait is as good as a letter
portraits give an empty comfort; letters carry real traces.
Seneca says the friend's own handwriting is the sweetest part
it's almost their hand itself, pressed onto the page.
the fortieth letter also talks about how fast to speak
a philosopher should speak slowly, not in a torrent.

games.q: you miss a faraway friend. you could send a quick photo, or write slowly by hand. what does the fortieth letter prize?
o: the letter in their hand: it carries real traces.
games.why: Seneca says pictures give an empty comfort; a letter brings real traces and marks of the absent friend.

practice: Think of one person far from you, by distance, by time or just by busyness, and picture their face, then their handwriting if you know it.
In your mind, begin a short note to them by hand: three or four slow sentences about what you'd want them to know today. If paper is nearby, you can start it now.

wordCard.voice: Real traces. Seneca says a friend's letter brings real traces of them, even their own hand, more than any portrait could. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the absent, present. A letter carries your traces, your own hand. Day four hundred fifty-nine, done.
